utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence. It still applies. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'll carry on from where I left off on our last sitting. Now, linked to the Serbian police force that expelled students of Albanian ethnicity from the university, can you tell us what came before that event and why the police took those steps.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The students and the professors had gone to classes as the regulations required. However, they were not allowed to do so by the police, and the police gave the reasons, that they had received orders not to leave them -- not to let them go into the classes. What preceded this wave of interruption of Albanian language classes was the introduction of violent measures, the suspension of even the last remaining autonomy which had been imposed by Serbian -- I'm referring here to the application of violent measures applied by Serbia in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the parallel system of education, and we're going to ask you briefly whether you agree with me on this: That a modern state, the kind that Serbia was at the time and exercised sovereign authority over the province, could finance such a system within a system when we're speaking about education.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not relevant what Serbia can fund or cannot fund. Kosova had its own institutions. Its institutions were suspended through violence, and, therefore, these institutions had to provide funding for Albanian language education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The students, you said, destroyed the technological faculty. Do you remember whether the police reacted on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one moment, the police intervened and got everybody out. The police removed all those students who refused to leave the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When we're on the subject of, if I can call it, the parallel system of education, in that parallel system of education was there any place for citizens of other ethnicities living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some involved in the parallel system. I'm referring here to some other citizens. There could have been, for example, Askali, Roma, Turks. The education which took part in Serbian language was funded by the Serbian institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I then conclude, and would you agree with me when I say the following: That it is correct that the Albanians after 1990 did not recognise the educational system of the Republic of Serbia? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is very clear that the introduction of the education system of Serbia in Kosova was an imposed system. The Albanian citizens in absolute majority refused this imposition, this forceful imposition, and the system which came with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like the usher to show us a document on the agreed measures to apply the agreement of the 1st of September, 1996, which was signed on the 23rd of March, 1998, and on e-court, I think it's D001-0011 in the Serbian version; D000-0013 in English. That's not the right document. Just a moment, please. The number of the document is 0001-0001. No. No, it's not the one on our screens. I'll be asking for that one to be put up later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And in English?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen that document before. Probably I have heard about it or maybe I saw it in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look and read out paragraph 4, since you say that you're not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only have paragraphs 1 to 3 on our screens now, but we'd like paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May we continue? My question is this: You heard that the Institute for Albanology was opened, that it started working, and I'd like to know what this institute dealt with, the Institute for Albanology.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very easy to say or to assume what this institute deals with. It deals with Albanian studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How many people began working in the institute, and what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did those people have salaries at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were paid by the parallel system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So that means when it came to financing, you're sure that it was financed from the parallel system, you say, or do you think? Do you know or do you think?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Republic of Serbia and before that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had a fund for financing the underdeveloped regions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're talking about a period which is completely different. You're speaking about a different time in Yugoslavia. The Albanological Institute began to be funded by the parallel system from the moment when the work of the institutions of Kosova was suspended. From that time on, the work of those institutions then began to get funding from the parallel system, including the Albanological system. I'm talking here about the period which starts from 1990. You, on the other hand, are talking about a fund for underdeveloped parts at the time when Tito was in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time in Serbia. At that time in Serbia too. I don't think you heard me. In 1998 do you know that a fund existed in the Republic of Serbia for financing the underdeveloped regions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Probably for development of a village in Serbia, but I think it would be cynical to say that there had been a fund for -- from Serbia for Kosova at the time when Serbia had occupied Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Republic of Serbia, from that same fund, invested considerable resources into Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have invested those funds for the Serbian population. Kosova as a country was paralysed at that time, so probably they had to fund the police action or the action of other institutions to keep in place this colonial regime in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time the Republic of Serbia fulfilled all its international obligations linked to loans?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Serbia had occupied Kosova, which means that they also carried over the loans of Kosova, the obligations that Kosova had to other countries. So Serbia had taken over probably these obligations of Kosova, so probably Serbia did this toward the international financial obligations -- institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber to admit the document and give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked D00001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask the usher to bring up the next exhibit, that is to say, the previous document that was shown on our screens, and it was D0001-0011 in Serbian and D0001-0013 in English. That's the document. May we have the English version, too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Surroi, are you familiar with this document? Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen that document; however, I have heard about the meeting with the EU representatives. I was informed by the EU representatives about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, I'd now like to ask you to take a look at this document and to tell me whether there are -- whether there were any reactions to this document and whether any of what is set out in the document was actually put into effect.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was an act of goodwill by the EU to assist in the process of normalisation of the educational system in Kosova through the institution of educational institutions in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So these resources, did they come to the place where they were intended to go?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some work had started; however, at the time we had the escalation of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Might this exhibit be given a number by the Trial Chamber, and I'd like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the demonstrations in Kosovo, I believe you remember that in Kosovo and Metohija it was both the Serbs and other ethnicities which demonstrated, and do you remember that those police reacted and that those citizens who demonstrated ended up in prison?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the reaction of the police was not equal. In terms of returning educational buildings, there was a demonstration; however, the reaction of the police did not resemble at all towards these demonstrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serb citizens were also taken to trial on the basis of the public law and order regulations and also pursuant to the criminal code of Serbia and the Autonomous Province of Kosovo, as it was at the time, for taking part in the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To which case are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most severe reaction of the Serb authorities was demonstrated in the demonstrations organised by Mr. Draskovic and the democratic opposition in Serbia that was demanding new elections, and at that time one citizen was killed in Belgrade. Afterwards, Mr. Milosevic placed the tanks in the streets of Belgrade. I would like to remember -- remind you, however, that this was a most severe demonstration and the largest of the Serbian opposition, where one person lost his life. And every life is important, but in Kosova, however, many more people were killed in less -- in smaller demonstrations compared to that one in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I'm sorry about all that, too, but what I wanted to hear from you is linked to the demonstrations that were held only in Kosovo. So when I'm referring to that, I'm referring to the Serb citizens, and you asked me about a specific case. Now, I'd like to remind you that at that time in the opposition, you had members of the Serbian Radical Party and Dr. Vojislav Seselj, an accused before this Tribunal. Do you know that at that time he, Mr. Seselj, because of the demonstrations in Gnjilane spent more than 60 days in detention and the deputy of the president of the Serbian Radical Party, Tomislav Nikolic, also, who at this point is the president of the Progressive Party. That's the new party and that's what it's called. Do you know about any of that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this event. I don't remember the days and the dates, but I do remember the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the refugee crisis, I'll go back to that briefly, and we're talking about the period before the so-called summer offensive, as you referred to it, of these police forces, but until the very end it wasn't clear whether it was the Serb police forces or whether the army was involved there, too, because in your testimony you used the words "military action," and then you mentioned the police. But I'll come back to that in due course, in just a moment. Anyway, you mentioned the liberation of Obilic. When you say liberation of Obilic, you mean the KLA which attacked Obilic, and you said "liberate Obilic," and after that it withdrew. Now, what I'm interested in is: Do you know that -- not Obilic. I meant, not Obilic, Orahovac. I apologise for having misspoken. Now, do you know -- well, everything that I was saying was referring to Orahovac. Do you know that on that occasion, 60 Serb citizens were seized, were abducted, just prior to that summer offensive?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, are you talking about Rahovec or Obiliq? I do not know the details of the activities of one or another party, but when I spoke of Rahovec, I described the created atmosphere immediately after the combat activities on behalf of the Serbian forces, after Rahovec was taken by the KLA, because the KLA had entered Rahovec. And with the ambassador and Mr. Shala, we visited the town. We saw people who were scared, we saw houses that had been burnt, and, therefore, we asked for the religious leader of Rahovec, who was a well-respected person at that time, and he was executed in the yard of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that event, but what my question was is: Do you know that during that action the KLA seized 60 Serbs? And I assume as a journalist at the head of a respected paper at the time and worked as a journalist, do you have that knowledge, and do you know about it or not? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, but I know that on this occasion we visited the Serbian neighbourhood in Rahovec and we spoke with the Serbs about these issues that you raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But what I'm asking you is: Do you know whether anybody was seized? You might not know the number, but do you know that this event took place, of this event?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that we did hear about cases of kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes it clearer now. Now, did you hear that after that a certain number of citizens of Orahovac who were Serbs, or, rather, their bodies were found in the Volujak pit, the Volujak cave?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of a case when bodies were found in several places in Kosova, including Voljak, after the war. Excuse me. I don't know whether these people were identified or not, these victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then, I can't ask the next question, which was to have been whether you knew that they were citizens from Orahovac. But anyway, my next question now is this: It will be linked to the mistake I made a moment ago when I misspoke and I spoke about the thermoelectric power station of Obilic. Do you know that the KLA at one point took control of the part of the installations of the thermoelectric power system of Obilic and cut off the transport to the coal that was supposed to be taken to the thermoelectric power plant?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on the news about the KLA units in Obiliq; however, I'm not familiar with their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard on the same news bulletin that nine workers of Serb ethnicity had been kidnapped on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem with the news at that time was the source, and it was very difficult to verify the credibility of events, such as this one in Obiliq. What we were able to do at that time was to report that according to the Serb media or Serb authorities or according to official sources of Serb authorities, nine or eight or seven, whatever the number of people, have been kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have your own sources of information?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that it was very difficult to penetrate to those areas -- in those areas where the conflict was ongoing, especially in those areas controlled by the Serb forces or encircled by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Had not the KLA occupied that area and expelled those people?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue is disputed. As you know, a person can occupy a point during one day and then withdraw the next. The KLA was not an army; it was a guerrilla movement and was not able to capture or control part of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I then conclude that you did not have your own sources of information to check that event?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't follow each and every combat activity in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to a different subject. You mentioned the law banning transactions in real estate, and you said that Albanians were prevented by this law from selling or buying real estate, and the purpose was to prevent them from buying property from Serbs. Now, I would like to ask you, was this law in effect, and was it applied throughout the territory of Serbia? Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it correctly, and this is just for purpose of an anecdote because I don't give it much relevance, at this time there was an initiative by Albanian lawyers to examine the constitutional aspect of this law. In Vojvodina, there was no such restriction on buying and selling property between different ethnicities, which means that this law was drafted specifically to prevent the buying and selling of property in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have to ask you this, then: Do you know that that particular law does not mention transactions in real estate between different ethnic groups? And do you know that the Serb lawyers, too, had initiated a constitutional review of that law?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well done by the Serb lawyers. It's a good thing they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that law did not contain provisions referring to ethnic communities and transactions between different ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The implementation of this law meant that the Albanian who wanted to buy property from a Serb in Kosova, he had to ask the Ministry of Finance in Belgrade for approval. And this ministry, then, in consulting with other ministries, would give the approval. I don't know if this is a direct implementation of the law or something else, but this is something that those who study laws and regulations should deal with. And it's not relevant for our discussion here today. This was a discrimination in transactions, and it was backed by law, by the law in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you now, are you going to agree with me that all the citizens of Serbia who wanted to buy or sell real estate needed to ask for that approval in Serbia proper and in Vojvodina, as well, and without such an approval, any contract on the purchase of real estate was not valid?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a different subject, the ethnic composition of Kosovo. You are talking about roughly 1990. Do you know, when was the last time when the Albanians participated in a census? Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a census in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts to carry out a census in 1991; however, at that time, due to the circumstances, a large number of citizens refused to participate in this census.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did not Albanians consider that to be an advantage for them, being in the majority?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statistics imposed by a country that uses force and violence and that was considered by the majority of Kosovans as foreign in Kosova, and this fear, general fear, of Albanians in Kosova meant that the registration in 1991 could be manipulated by the Serb authorities in order to create fictitious statistical data that would later be used in different shapes and forms. This fear built up after a campaign by the Serb media, claiming that the increase of the birth-rate of the Albanians is a product of a doctrine that intends to over-populate a territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I could perhaps even agree with you that that was one of the possible viewpoints, but I would like to move on to the part of your statement where you say there were about 85 per cent ethnic Albanian citizens to 95 per cent ethnic Albanians and 5 per cent Serbs. I would like to know the basis for that statement and how well-founded, how sure you are about this estimate, since you put it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a contradiction in your question. You cannot make a precise forecast because forecasting in its nature can never be precise. This, what I'm talking about, is a projection on demographic growth. Demographers at the time agreed on this issue, and these figures were calculated on the basis of the natural norm of birth-rate since 1981. And based on the mortality rate and also based on the migration rate, you could come to the conclusion that sometime in 1985 the majority was Albanian. In the registration -- in the census of 1991, though the Albanians did not take part in the census, the Serbs took part. And again, I will point out here that I'm speaking in terms of demography; there was a trend of increased birth-rate but also a trend of migration and movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On this topic, my last question: You will agree with me that the birth-rate in Kosovo, speaking of the ethnic Albanian community, for the past ten years has been the highest in Europe.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe not only in the last ten years but even more. These were demographic trends that other nations went through earlier. This is not a specialty for the Albanians only. I would like to remind you that in early twentieth century, a birth-rate of this size was evident for Norway, and this birth-rate, after social and economic development, reached the trend of the average European country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked this because of its relevance to the period only. I'll now move on to another subject. You said that in July 1990, the members of the parliament of Kosovo adopted a so-called constitutional declaration - when I say "members of the parliament of Kosovo," I mean ethnic Albanian MPs - proclaiming Kosovo a republic within the Yugoslav federation. Tell me, who were those members of the assembly at that time? I would like an answer in general terms.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were those who were elected at that time. At the time, we did not have direct elections; however, in those conditions these people were elected as members of parliament, who represented Kosova, as it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were they ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were Albanians; however, there were also Turkish citizens who had signed that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the translation, and I believe that it is a mistake. It's not "Turkish citizens"; it's "citizens of Turkish ethnicity."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned September of 1990 and the movement for independence and the referendum for independence. Did only ethnic Albanians participate in that referendum, or did all citizens participate?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I have not counted the participants; however, by chance the neighbour of my mother - she is a Serb - she also took part in the vote and voted in favour of the independence of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that neighbour? Last name?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mohn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... Albanian?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In May 1990, there were parliamentary elections and presidential elections for Kosovo and Metohija, and Dr. Ibrahim Rugova had a land-slide victory in the presidential election. How many members of parliament who were elected in that election were of Serb ethnicity, if any?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Turks elected as members. There was no Serb elected; however, their seats were provided as vacant in the parliament of Kosova. These were seats designed for the citizens of Serbian ethnicity. So if they wanted to be elected, they could be elected for those seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know and will you agree with me that at that time under the federal criminal code, such activity related to the organising of parliamentary elections in circumvention of the existing legislation was found to be a criminal act, a subversion of the federal system and the constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no federation as such at that time. From the decision of the Badinter Commission, the Yugoslav socialist republic had died, or judicially this republic had been declared as dead. That period, from the moment when the death of this country was declared until the birth of the new states, is a provisional period, a transitional period, during which the federation, which you called as Yugoslav socialist republic, was a violent creation -- was a forced creation set up to justify the military actions of the Serbian regime, as well as to cover up the occupation of Kosova. At the moment when socialist Yugoslavia was declared as dead was a moment in which all the peoples and the units that existed within that federation at that time to make -- to take decisions on their own future. Kosova, on 2 July 1990, and also through its referendum, declared the will of the people of Kosova, and this will was in favour of independence. So I think it's totally irrelevant to refer to what other institutions might have decided at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you again. Under the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, do you know that such activities were a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not set up on the basis of the will of the people of Kosova, and the citizens of Kosova have not accepted this creature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand that. I'm not going to repeat my question again because we have that law here, and in some other part of this trial we will tender it as evidence. So I'm not going to insist any more. I will only ask you, as a follow-up to my previous question, since you are well known as a man working for democratic values for a long time, I'll ask you: Do you believe elections to be democratic if only ethnic Albanian citizens participated in the elections? You mentioned a couple of ethnic Turks but ...

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would reformulate my answer. On the basis of the OSCE standards, these were not free and fair elections; however, again, on basis of the standards, those elections were even freer and fairer than those held in Serbia, even though those elections took place under occupation conditions. However, what should never be doubted is that there was an expression of will by the citizens for independence and the people, even though the conditions were so bad, were willing to contribute to holding those elections. It's just like a soccer game. If you go to the stadium and still refuse to play football, then the consequences are there for you to suffer under FIFA regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think FIFA rules were applied in this case, but let's move on. You mentioned the Bertelsmann Research Foundation. Since you participated in its work, who is the founder and the financier of this organisation?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Mohn family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if it was really a case of legitimate negotiation between the delegations of Serbia and the delegation of Kosova - you mentioned Rhodes and some other places; you mentioned Simic and other participants from the Serb side - but as far as I remember, and I hope you will agree, that both of them were members of the opposition at that time. They were not represented in the government, not even this new democracy about which you said that Mihajlovic, who was the leader of that party, had access to Milosevic, they did not participate in the government too. They were in opposition.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think something should be corrected in your question. I did not say that these were negotiations between Kosova and Serbia. These were "track 2" negotiations, that is, negotiations in the second channel, if we could put it that way. So people who were interested in such talks or, let's say, civil society, people thought that they could use this opportunity to contribute to the creation of a kind of framework for what should have been later official negotiations. These meetings, this dialogue which took place with the assistance of Bertelsmann, were never considered as a process of negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have clarified this point, and I will have no further questions on that. I had to cover this ground because of the response that is on the record from your previous testimony. I will now go back to the case of the Jashari family. You said that Adem Jashari was one of the founders of the KLA, and I agree about that, and you said that before that he was a well-known activist in this area. You meant Prekaz and Drenica and that area. Activist of what kind?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he could have been an activist of the Democratic League or any other party. But what I could say was that he was a person well known in those -- in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On this point, when we're talking specifically about Adem Jashari, do you know that he was under investigation by the competent authorities at the time, it was a criminal investigation, and that he was even convicted?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information at that time. It's clear that Mr. Jashari was a person wanted by the police. In the final analysis, the siege proved this. As far as the conviction is concerned, this was mentioned by Mr. Milosevic at the meeting he had with us. He described him as criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But he said that, that Milosevic said that, not that he did or didn't, but that Milosevic said that. You said that members of the Jashari family were called upon to surrender, not surrender their arms but to surrender. We know that they did not do that. Now, do you know that there was fighting between the forces of law and order and the Jashari family? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt that there was an exchange of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that several policemen were seriously wounded on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt it either. Mr. Jashari had declared earlier that he would fight till his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Albanian on English channel) [Previous translation continues] ... that at those journalists of yours were very frequently accompanied journalist from foreign news agencies, and that they were valuable assistants to the foreign journalists for them to be able to pass through the blockades and check-points along the roads. Now, who had all those blockades? Who had control of the check-points?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... vice versa. The foreign journalists were a big help for our journalists to get access because the check-points on those roads were also controlled by the Serbian police. There were also check-points set up by KLA, no doubt about that. However, I don't believe that the KLA obstructed the access to the media because I think that it was in the interests of the KLA to ensure that these views, these pictures, reached the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, while we're on the subject -- well, I'll move on to another area, the negotiations, starting with G15 through G5, the Rambouillet negotiators and the negotiations in Paris. I think I'm going to surprise you with the very few number of questions I have on that topic, but I do believe that they are key questions. Now, did you ever, since 1997, as a delegation - and I'm asking you that because you took part in all these events, G15, G5, Rambouillet, Paris - as a delegation, therefore, a delegation of Albanians, Kosovars, Albanians from Kosovo, did you have any lesser demand than full independence for Kosovo and Metohija, either through peaceful negotiations, democratic institutions, up to a referendum, or, as some members thought, by armed struggle? Did you ever have a lesser demand than complete independence?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only from 1997 but from 1991, there was a consensus in our society that Kosova should be independent. This consensus was reflected by us who were engaged in negotiations, and we tried to defend that consensus in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. It's quite clear, in view of the referendum that was held, but I wanted to hear it from you. Now, were you a participant in all these negotiations directly, as a representative of the Albanian nation, independently, you said. So when I'm asking you that, I'm talking about G15, G5, Rambouillet, and Paris. You yourself, personally.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I also have to tell you that I'm grateful to you for the answer you gave with respect to the Rambouillet meeting, and later, the Paris one too. Now, the essence of what I want to say is this: You clearly said that the representatives of the Serb delegation were offered an agreement by which the state would give up its territory - you didn't say that but that is what is contained in the provisions of the agreement, deferred, of course - and that the state would be bombed unless the agreement were accepted, which in my opinion was contrary to international law and customs and represents quite literally coercion, brutal coercion, with the threat of the greatest force behind it from the greatest power; or to use the language used by the army, an ultimatum before a war. So would you agree with me there that that was what the situation was when it came to the Serb negotiators in Rambouillet, and then especially so subsequently in Paris?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you have a description which is closer to the description of your officials, a description they stuck to for many years. I'd like now to give you a description which is not that conventional. The Serbian delegation which represented a state that had exercised systematically, and was continuing to do that, violence against people in Kosova, so that country was given the opportunity to end this systematic violence by signing a contract with international community and the representatives of Kosova. That contract would give Serbia the occasion to have a limited army and police presence for a limited period of time, a process for the protection of the Serbian cultural and religious heritage, a process for the protection of Serbian citizens who were in a minority in Kosova, a process for rebuilding the democratic institutions in which the Serbian citizens would be represented, and a peaceful process through which Kosova would ultimately take its decision on its status. This would have been done on the basis of all of this contract. This interpretation would mean that Serbia would be rewarded for taking a democratic step and for deciding to put an end to the regime of occupation and repression of Albanian people in Kosova. Otherwise, if Serbia would refuse to take such a democratic path, would have been penalised, that is, the genocide which was being prepared by Serbia in Kosova would have been penalised. So this is a description which I think is closer to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you on that point, since the heritage of a modern civilisation, particularly when we talk about democracy, implies negotiation, first of all, talks, and so on, whereas your answer contains what the previous position was, that the Albanian nationality had a clear-cut stand in 1990 for complete independence, regardless of what would happen. But I don't want to enter into polemics with you on that. I'd just like to ask you this: Did you hold negotiations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on that occasion or with Serbia? I mean Rambouillet and Paris, there.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, you could describe it as you wish, but it's difficult to say to what extent the delegation was a delegation of federal Yugoslavia or Serbia. But Montenegro was not represented there, even though Montenegro formally still belonged to that unnatural federation between Serbia and Montenegro. Therefore, realistically speaking, there was only one address for the negotiations, and the address was in Belgrade. The man who was there was Slobodan Milosevic. He was the only person who was the man charged with taking decisions on his country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But we can conclude that you nonetheless held negotiations with Serbia, and Slobodan Milosevic was president at that time of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that President Milosevic at that time didn't have the legitimacy to negotiate on behalf of Montenegro, which was also there as a state within the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that the President of the Republic of Serbia at that time, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, who took part in the negotiations throughout.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of negotiations in Paris, Mr. Milutinovic shrugged his shoulders and said he could not take any decision because it was his boss who took decisions on those issues, and his boss was Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did he say that too?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said these words to the mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, linked to the agreements - Rambouillet, Paris, and everything that you went through with the delegation of Albanians from Kosovo - I'm going to ask you this: In testifying today before this Tribunal, can you really consider yourself to be objective and unbiased as a witness, whereas you represented the interests of only the Albanians throughout, Albanians from Kosovo? Isn't that, in a certain sense, a conflict of interest?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My coming here to this Tribunal is in the quality of a witness. I have come here to testify. I'm here to be asked by you, and I'm here to answer your questions. I have not come here to demonstrate an absence or presence of conflict of interest. I've come here to tell you whatever you ask me for, without any discrimination to the truth. So this is why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course everybody here would like that to be the case. Now, Mr. Surroi, I'm going to leave that topic and move on to another area with other questions. Precisely because of the answer I've just been given, I'm going to skip over a whole series of questions that I had intended to ask you, and what I'm now going to ask you relates to what you stated earlier in other cases that are considered relevant cases, your testimony in the -- well, in a case that was known as the Milosevic case, the Milosevic trial, and your testimony in the Milutinovic et al trial. Answer me this: Since I have studied the transcripts from those trials, tell me why, then, didn't you mention the story about the thrown-away ID cards that you saw on the streets of Pristina and about the house of your childhood friend, the scene when you entered the house of your childhood friend and saw the hot cake and so on? How come it's only after all this time that you happen to remember things like that, if I can call them details, that you didn't mention in trials which, during the pre-trial, were considered to be far more important than what we're talking about now, the period that we're discussing now?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no -- there is no specific reason. Memory is not a straightforward line. The memory occurs in different contexts. So it's in this context, if you ask me for many other issues, I could talk to you about other issues which I've not mentioned on any other occasions. My life experience is much broader than the framework of questions and answers in this judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Albanians rejoiced but were also concerned when the NATO bombing started. Now I'm going to ask you this: Do you know how many civilians were killed in Kosovo? I'm not going to ask you about ethnic Albanians. Just generally, how many civilians were killed in Kosovo, at least roughly speaking, a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the people who were killed were civilians in Kosova. Most of the people killed by the Serbian forces were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was clear to you that the context of my question was the bombing by NATO. That's what I was asking you about.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The gravest incidents in regard to the NATO bombing was in the village of Korisha, where more than 100 people were killed. The proportion of people killed by the NATO bombing to the number of people killed by the Serbian forces is clearly -- is huge, so if you compare this number of 100 people to more than 10.000 people killed. So you can see the context, as far as numbers are concerned, we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Kosovo several thousand Serbs disappeared and their remains were never found. Some were; some weren't. But anyway that number disappeared.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of those who disappeared is huge. I'm speaking about citizens of Kosova. The majority of those missing are Albanians, and there is quite a number of Serbian citizens of Kosova who are missing. According to the information that I last read, the number in total of those missing and who have not been identified or found is 2.500 of both ethnic groups. The Serb civilians are difficult to be found due to the fact that their bodies were not put in a collective grave. The Albanian bodies, by those who deal with these issues, can be easily identified in the mass graves in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Do you know that the number of civilians who were killed during the NATO bombing - I'm not going to use -- I'm not going to say whether they were killed by Albanians or the NATO pact - but do you know that the number of Serbs in relation to the population, the Serb population, in Kosovo percentage-wise is much higher than the number of Albanian civilians who disappeared? I'm not going to say whether they were killed by the Serb forces or NATO. In relation to the figures you mentioned and statistics, would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not clear whether you're referring to the victims of bombing or to the kidnapping of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about general things. A dead man, a dead man is a very sad thing, whether the person was killed as a result of NATO's action, depleted uranium, or by somebody's hand in retaliation for some other death or for political reasons. I'm not going into any of that. I'm just looking at the number of people killed in one way or another. Their bodies were not found; they went missing. So what I asked you in that context is this: Would you agree that the number of Serbs who were killed in Kosovo in relation to the overall number of Serbs living in Kosovo, the Serb population is many times more than the number and percentage of Albanians killed in relation to the percentage of Albanians living in Kosovo, so in relative terms?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. And you should divide the combat activities into several phases. We deal here with details that I'm not quite familiar with. I'm not that precise when it comes to statistics in terms of these events. From 1998 to March 1999, then the phase from the beginning of the NATO campaign, 24th March-June 1999, and the redistribution [as interpreted] phase and the entire summer of 1999, so I think you will agree that there existed an organised state instrument that persecuted Albanian citizens. There were combat activities. There was war that damaged, cause damage to the citizens, and there existed a retribution movement that also caused damage to a number of citizens of Serbian ethnicity, and I think this is more important than the statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I think I would require another 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honours, to complete my cross-examination, and I think that this is a good time, before I move on to another area, to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will certainly accommodate that suggestion, Mr. Djordjevic, and we will have our first break now, resuming at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the legal officer to bring up the map of Kosovo. That's 65 ter 00044.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, we now all see on the screens the map of Kosovo. We see that in the central part of Kosovo there is Pristina, although it's a bit to the east, but we see the town of Pec in the centre. Since you worked as a reporter, as a journalist, I suppose you are aware that just before the summer offensive, there were barricades and roadblocks on the Pristina-Pec road in 1998.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this map, kindly tell us, since you still lived there, how was one able to go to Pec from Pristina at that time in one's own car, without encountering any roadblocks, army check-points, guerilla fighters, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To travel without problem at the time was impossible. There were blockades, check-points, patrols everywhere. Therefore, any movement in Kosova took three or four times more time than usual. I already told you that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but let me be more precise. If you were, for instance, an ethnic Serb and you want to arrive safely to Pec and you know there are roadblocks would you agree with me that from Pristina you would go first to the north, to Zvecani; and then via Sandzak, Tutin you would go to Rozaj; and then from Rozaj via Kuljaj you would go to Pec. That's what ethnic Serbs did to avoid the roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This route was possible, but as I told you, it took four or five times longer to make that travelling. It was difficult for both Serbians and the Albanians to travel around at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it the same with the Suva Reka-Pristina road in 1998, just before the summer?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that ethnic Serbs travelled from Suva Reka to Pristina by going first south towards Prizren, Strpce, Urosevac and only then to Pristina, instead of going directly from Suva Reka to the north towards Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it would be helpful in this trial to provide estimations about routes in Kosova. But I could also give you details about a route which I followed in order to go to Junik together with Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Shala. We had to go from Prishtina towards south in the direction of Ferizaj, and then we took the western direction for the Sharr mountains. In the direction from Prizren, we were stopped several times by the Serbian police. Then from Prizren to Gjakova , we were stopped by Serbian police, and then from Gjakova, we went to Junik. This route under normal circumstances would take only one hour and 45 minutes. At that time we did it -- even though we were provided access in most of the cases, despite the stops by the police, we reached our destination after five hours. So I think you should agree that it was difficult for any Kosovar citizen to travel around at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As you mentioned, Ambassador Holbrooke and you were traveling to Junik. Did you travel in cars with diplomatic licence plates?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the US embassy car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, can I conclude that you were not supposed to have any problems, either with Serb police check-points or the KLA check-points?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, under normal circumstances there should have been no problem; however, we were still stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Trial Chamber to admit this map and to assign it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, during the NATO air-strikes, were civilian facilities targeted, such as private houses of Albanians, factories, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the bombs fell in the post office of Prishtina. This was the only bomb that fell in Prishtina and in a civilian facility. As I told you earlier, there were two or three or more incidents in which the columns of people with tractors were bombarded. These tractors, this convoy of people, in the case of Korisha, these were people who were expelled from their village, from Korisha. They were forcefully ordered to go towards Albania. Then they were forced to go back, and while they were stopping at the village of Korisha, they were bombarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the legal officer to bring up photographs of the centre of Pristina, D001-2868/2869, first 2868 and then 2869.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, you see here three photographs. Can you give us a very brief comment on what you see?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photo on the left is the Kosova post office building. Now it's a building used by Kosova government. That building suffered damage in the window, in those -- the post was bombarded at night. The post is pictured on the right above. That night when the post was shelled, I was about 1 kilometre away, as the crow flies, so I heard the bomb when it fell. The photograph on the right-hand corner is a shopping mall in Prishtina. The windows were also broken of this facility as a result of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask, the next photograph, 2869. D001-2869.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This house is next to the post office, which was hit as a result of the bombing of the post, and a very old family from Prishtina was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All these photographs depict that one house?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a street, an old street in Prishtina with old infrastructure. Now, whether it is just one house or more, that I don't know. But I know that in this particular house there were civilian victims of this bombing, civilians, members of an old family from Prishtina who were killed during the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Surroi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender these two sets of photographs and to have numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the two sets of photographs as they've been displayed, including the text.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D001-2868 will be assigned D00004; and the other one, which is identified as D001-2869, will be assigned D00005.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for a video-clip to be played of the ABC television, marked as D001-2870, and another video-clip from Studio B, a local Belgrade television. Since we know that the witness understands and speaks English fluently, I would like him to listen to the recording, and once we have seen the video-clip, I would like his brief comment. He has already said a few words about this without any question from the Defence, but I would like a comment on the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It's not ABC; it's BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I should intervene regarding the minutes of the trial. It is not BBC; it is ABC broadcasting television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, a moment ago you were talking about this incident. My first question: Was this a convoy of Albanians going back to their houses, who were not on their way to Albania?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question. This is a documentary. You cannot hear any description of the incident, and you cannot identify whether this refers to one village or another village, so I cannot give you any specific answer. However, two things come on the surface from this documentary. First, throughout the bombing campaign, I was in Prishtina, and I was able to follow even the Serb media in relation to what was going on at the time. It is not honest to show on the Serb national media, to demonstrate a concern for the Albanian nation when at the same time the same state demonstrated terror over the Albanian population. But this all was war propaganda, and that cannot be explained in rational terms here. Secondly, the question posed here is, why were these citizens forced to leave their village and to form this convoy of tractors? That answer is very simple. They were forced to leave their homes. This violence was being exercised in continuity for years by the Serb police, by the Serb authorities. Eventually, many of these villages were emptied, following direct orders of police commanders, Serb police commanders, who knocked on the doors and told the people to pack up their things and leave in a matter of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you looked at this video-clip carefully, did you notice members of the Serbian police carrying the wounded, a Serb policeman carrying an Albanian child, Serbian policemen helping people evacuate and find shelter?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're talking about a documentary that is out of context, which is not defined in terms of time and space, illustrated by radiophonic communication between pilots and bases. So I see the purpose of this documentary and, as I said, it is a product of a period of time when propaganda was being launched. As I said, I understand the purpose of the propaganda, but I don't justify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, the truth of this documentary is precisely a document about a horrible truth, not propaganda. I don't want to say horrible to whom and why. This video-clip was filmed on the 7th of April, 1998. It's the environs of Meja village. It's a convoy of Albanian refugees, and on that point I'll agree with you, who were on their way to their homes, targeted by NATO from 1330 until 1530, for a full two hours, although the pilot said to his base, as we could hear clearly from this video-clip - the base was called Mother - the pilot said he thought he could see civilians, and, nevertheless, he received orders to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not comment, myself, on this video-clip. I will just ask the Trial Chamber to admit this video-clip and to assign it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, please. I cannot make any comments because other bodies should be there to define the quality of this documentary. Since you mentioned the village of Meja, this village is known not for the NATO bombing. It is better known because of the execution of civilians, of all those men who were separated from their children, of the elderly people separated from the convoy and executed. More than 100 people from this village, from this incident, were -- are still missing, and their families cannot bury their remains. So I pose here the same question: What made these people leave their villages and set off for Albania, escorted by the Serb forces? What made them return from Albania, back? It's not their own free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the video has some difficulties about its understanding and interpretation at the moment. The witness does not recognise the location. Clearly, the soundtrack has nothing to do with what is being depicted in -- both in time and in circumstance. The Chamber would certainly be prepared to have the video-clip marked for identification at this stage, but it will be necessary for other evidence to indicate what is the subject matter of the video and how it relates to our concerns in this case. So if you're content with that, we'll mark it for identification at this time, but we have flagged that we will need other evidence to enable us to know what it is that is being depicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll agree with you, Your Honour. The Defence, too, had a great deal of problem in identifying all this material, but we will, in the time we have, to ensure that we have exhibits and material relating to the concrete exhibit. But for the moment, we are satisfied with what we've just heard Your Honour to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have this video-clip marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00006, MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have another video-clip shown on e-court. It is D0001-0696.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, I think you are familiar with this footage. You haven't got it on your screen yet. Anyway, it's the visit by Ambassador Holbrooke to the village of Junik in 1998, in the month of June. Yes, here we have the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You can see yourself on that footage. Do you agree that that was you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I'm interested in is this: What was the purpose of Ambassador Holbrooke's visit to the village of Junik in 1998, in June?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, professor Agani, Mr. Shala, and I asked Ambassador Holbrooke to see, in concrete terms on the field, what was going on in Kosova. As I said, our journey took us quite awhile, four hours, to arrive to that part of Kosova, western part, where fighting was going on. So we wanted to see with our own eyes what was going on in those parts where the war and combat activities had escalated. At the time, in June and July of that year, we - that is, part of the Kosovan delegation - were trying to unify the political positions of the Albanians of Kosova so that -- with the aim to unify the two wings - the wing of the passive resistance headed by Mr. Rugova and the armed wing, the KLA wing. So we had information about the developments within the ranks of the Kosova Liberation Army. So at that time, we went to the village of Junik. We were received by this organised military structure. We sat and had a talk. We were informed about what was going on in that particular village, and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On that same occasion did you happen to visit, for example, some headquarters of the Serb police and army that was in the war zone? Did you go there together with Ambassador Holbrooke when you went to visit representatives of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before arriving at part of Gjakova municipality, we stopped at a junction between Prishtina, Prizren, and Gjakova, and we came across an armed and fortified roadblock of the Serbian police forces. Upon the insistence of Ambassador Holbrooke, the two of us got out of the car and spoke with the commander of the police forces who was controlling that part of the area, and he explained to us the position of the police, the Serbian police, and the Serbian state, their tactics, and their -- then the purpose of their presence in that part of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, that commander of the Serb police, did he introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably he did, but I do not remember the name. When I asked him as to why he was there, he said that he was there to defend the Catholic village from the KLA that, in his words, was a fundamentalist and Islamic military organisation. But when I said to him that the commander of that area, the KLA commander was a Catholic one, he said -- and when I told him that many KLA leaders were of Catholic religion, he then turned to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that connection, I'd like to ask you this: Would you agree with me when I say that the activities of the Serbian police at that time in that area was to deblock the roads and communication lines without entering into Albanian villages, or not, when we're talking about the Pec-Djakovica road via Decani, for example?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I clearly understood your question, in that period of time, and as I said I'm not well informed of all the armed activities, but if my recollection serves me right, there was an order at the time to create a corridor, a 5-kilometre corridor, from the Albanian border, a security corridor, security belt. So from Decan to Gjakova, the whole border area of 5 kilometres was comprised. The aim of this roadblock was, in my opinion, to control this border belt, extending to Has from the direction of Prizren, and then joined with the mountain part of Gjakova and Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 38, line 5: Instead of "KLA leader," I would like to say "KLA soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, I'd like to tender the video into evidence, and I'd like it to be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along with the note that it was without audio-tape, without an audio signal. And as I'm drawing to the end of my cross-examination, I'd just like to say that all the D4 and D5 exhibits linked to the Defence case, I'd like to say that the Defence is only asking the admission into evidence of the photographs, without the text below, which is in Serbian, in the Cyrillic script. So just the visual images. And bringing my cross-examination to a close, I'd just like to return to Pristina, and as the witness said, the retribution of the Serbs after the first night of the bombing or, rather, the beginning of the bombing, by NATO, we all remember full well that he said in his testimony that those who had icons were spared; those who did not have icons were not spared. And the Prosecutor directly, when it came to the question of icons, used the adjective "Orthodox."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that connection, I would like to ask the witness the following: Can he give us an answer as to whether, except for the Albanians who are Muslims, whether there are Christians, Catholic Muslims and even Orthodox --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Albanians, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- Catholic, Christian, Albanians, and Orthodox Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosova, there could be two Albanian Orthodox whom I know. As far as the Catholics are concerned, their share of the population could be around 10 per cent. Mr. Djordjevic, the icon is not part of the Catholic religious tradition. The icon exists in most of the cases in our religion traditions, starting from the Byzantine times, so it exists in the Orthodox religious rites. Therefore, the display of the icons on those days in Prishtina was an intention to display religious affiliation. So the protection which was provided through the icon was through this religious identification. So it was used as a means of protection, used by the Serbs to protect themselves from the wave of destruction, and in fact it was good for them to use this means as a way of protecting themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will agree with you that the icons are, first and foremost, a reflection of the Orthodox traditions and Byzantine culture and so on. But let me remind you that Catholics also have images of Mary and Christ and that those, too, are images or icons, iconos from the Greek, which means image, picture. Now, what about the aethiasts? There are quite a few communists among the Serbs in Kosovo, more than Albanians.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any display of the five-cornered star -- five-edges star to be used on those days as a means of protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a picture of Josip Bros Tito. All right. I don't want to go into that now. But I'd like you to explain a phenomenon, which I don't understand, and I'll wind up with that, and I see this today, a phenomenon which is not very clear to me, but I'm sure that you'll have some explanation that will wind up my cross-examination for today. Far before the conflicts broke out, I went to Kosovo many times as a lawyer and even during the war, and I have been Defence counsel, as well, for this Tribunal. But what I would see all the time, even before the conflict, were flags of the Republic of Albania in Kosovo, displayed in Kosovo, at weddings, at any joyous occasions or other ceremonies, perhaps sad ones, too, or elections; I would see Albanian flags flown in Kosovo, the Republic of Albania, I mean, and I still see that in western Macedonia, for example. I see elections, and the flag flown is the flag of the Republic of Albania. Do you think that is normal for the attributes of another state and country to be displayed in another state? I'd like to hear your explanation because I consider you to be a man of integrity and a well-educated man. So could you explain that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration. Initially, it was the flag. Then the state came. The Albania flag, as it is, displayed from the times of Skanderbeg and held up during the Albanian wars against the Ottoman Empire. This was a flag which existed before any form of Albanian status existed. The fact that the Republic of Albania in a natural way adopted this as the national flag does not mean that the Republic of Albania has adopted in a natural way the whole Albanian nation. Part of the Albanian nation not in a natural way has remained outside the borders of Albania, which means that those who remained outside Albania had the right to use the national flag, just like the state used it, the Albanian state used it as its national symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd now like to go on to another question. Ethnologically, Albanian -- an Albanian means a citizen of the Republic of Albania. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the components of the Albanian is being a citizen of Albania. However, being Albanian is a national identity, not only a state identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this: How do Albanians in Albanian call the Republic of Albania? What's the Albanian's name for the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Albania, the Republika Shqiperise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian. Shqiptar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: So that is their own name for themselves, Shqiperise. The question not interpreted, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank the Trial Chamber. That completes my cross-examination. I'd like to thank Mr. Veton Surroi as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Could I mention that the Chamber has received the photographs which were tendered clearly as extracts from some publication. We have received the pages as they were displayed, and that includes the text. If there is agreement from the Prosecution, we could receive them without the text, but otherwise, we receive the exhibit as it was shown and tendered. Clearly, though, the evidence has not sought to explain or comment upon the text that it's displayed, so the Chamber would not be able to attach any weight to the text at the moment. But formally, it is received as part of the exhibit that was displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, Your Honours, there is one -- another intervene. [Interpretation] We have here in the transcript that there was no interpretation of my last question. It is page 42, line 6, at 11.50 and 24 seconds. It says "[No interpretation]," "Q" and then "[No interpretation]." Now, my question was this: How do you refer to yourselves, your Albanians? How do you call yourselves in your own language? What word do you use?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djordjevic. That will enable the completion of the transcript, and the account you've just given accords generally with my recollection of it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Surroi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the transcript, as well, at 42, 7, my answer is: "A. Albanian." And then "Siptar," which is not spelled properly. The proper spelling of "Shqiptar" as we call ourselves is S-h-q-i-p-t-a-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Ms. Kravetz, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll be pleased to know, Mr. Surroi, that that concludes the questions of you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance and for the assistance you've been able to give us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- during the process of questioning that has taken place. You may now, of course, leave and go about your ordinary affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours, I think I should mention quickly, before anything is done, that the next witness has protective measures in place, so we would need to go into closed session before he is brought in. I don't want him to be brought in before we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will just check on the nature of the protective measures, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be necessary for the Chamber to adjourn for some 20 minutes to enable physical screens and electronic protective measures to be put in place. The Chamber would then resume the hearing. That will leave us just one and a half hours to the end of the day's session, so it will work out reasonably well in practice. We will adjourn now and resume at a quarter past 12.00, by which time the protective measures should be in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're ready with the next witness, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That is K83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll move into closed session, then, to enable the witness to come in. Then we will go into public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, open session. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown document 02352.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does that document contain a description of your identity?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours, could the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
